{{Short description|Similarity measure between two invertible matrices}}
The '''Amari distance''',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Póczos |first=Barnabás |last2=Takács |first2=Bálint |last3=Lőrincz |first3=András |date=2005 |editor-last=Gama |editor-first=João |editor2-last=Camacho |editor2-first=Rui |editor3-last=Brazdil |editor3-first=Pavel B. |editor4-last=Jorge |editor4-first=Alípio Mário |editor5-last=Torgo |editor5-first=Luís |title=Independent Subspace Analysis on Innovations |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11564096_71 |journal=Machine Learning: ECML 2005 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=698–706 |doi=10.1007/11564096_71 |isbn=978-3-540-31692-3|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=R Graphical Manual – Compute the 'Amari' distance between two matrices|url=http://rgm3.lab.nig.ac.jp/RGM/R_rdfile?f=ProDenICA/man/amari.Rd&d=R_CC|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150109133357/http://rgm3.lab.nig.ac.jp/RGM/R_rdfile?f=ProDenICA%2Fman%2Famari.Rd&d=R_CC|archive-date=2015-01-09|access-date=2019-05-16}}</ref> also known as '''Amari index'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sobhani |first=Elaheh |last2=Comon |first2=Pierre |last3=Jutten |first3=Christian |last4=Babaie-Zadeh |first4=Massoud |date=2022-06-01 |title=CorrIndex: A permutation invariant performance index |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03230210v2/file/Final_version.pdf |journal=Signal Processing |language=en |volume=195 |article-number=108457 |doi=10.1016/j.sigpro.2022.108457 |issn=0165-1684|doi-access=free }}</ref> and '''Amari metric'''<ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Hastie | first1 = Trevor
 | last2 = Friedman | first2 = Jerome
 | last3 = Tibshirani | first3 = Robert
 | doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-84858-7
 | edition = 2nd
 | series = Springer Series in Statistics
 | publisher = Springer New York
 | title = The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction
 | url = https://hastie.su.domains/Papers/ESLII.pdf
 | year = 2009}}</ref> is a [[similarity measure]] between two [[invertible matrices]], useful for checking for convergence in [[independent component analysis]] algorithms and for comparing solutions. It is named after Japanese information theorist [[Shun'ichi Amari]] and was originally introduced as a performance index for [[blind source separation]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amari |first=Shun-ichi |last2=Cichocki |first2=Andrzej |last3=Yang |first3=Howard |date=1995 |title=A New Learning Algorithm for Blind Signal Separation |url=http://papers.nips.cc/paper/1115-a-new-learning-algorithm-for-blind-signal-separation.pdf |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |publisher=MIT Press |volume=8}}</ref>

For two invertible matrices <math>A, B \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</math>, it is defined as:

:<math>d(A, B) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{|p_{ij}|}{\max_{k} |p_{ik}|} - 1\right) + \sum_{j=1}^n \left(\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{|p_{ij}|}{\max_{k} |p_{kj}|} - 1\right),  P = A^{-1}B </math>

It is non-negative and cancels if and only if <math>A^{-1}B</math> is a scale and permutation matrix, i.e. the product of a [[diagonal matrix]] and a [[permutation matrix]]. The Amari distance is invariant to permutation and scaling of the columns of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bach |first=Francis R. |last2=Jordan |first2=Michael I. |date=2002 |title=Kernel Independent Component Analysis |url=https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/v3/bach02a.html |journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research |volume=3 |issue=Jul |pages=1–48 |issn=1533-7928}}</ref>
